title: What can we say about these leaning parallelograms?
description: Seven parallelograms stand on equal bases between the same two grid lines, some upright and some leaning far over. The board compares their areas by base and height, then compares their perimeters through the slanting sides, which grow as a shape leans.
teaching_notes: One idea: the same base and the same height give the same area, but the perimeter changes with the slanting sides. Watch for students who think equal areas mean equal perimeters.

video_script.why: The child uses area as base times height from the solved example to see why leaning parallelograms keep their area, while their perimeters change.
video_script.substitution: Compare base and height for the areas, then compare the slanting sides for the perimeters.
video_script.anchor: the book's row of parallelograms on a grid, on equal bases between the same two grid lines
video_script.payoff_line: All the parallelograms have equal areas

final_answer.spoken: the areas are equal and the perimeters differ

hold_back: All the parallelograms have equal areas
maths_rules: every parallelogram has the same base length b and the same height h, the distance between the two grid lines
area = base × height = b × h for every one, so all the areas are equal
perimeter = 2 × base + 2 × slanting side, and the base is the same for all
slanting side = square root of (h² + s²), where s is the sideways shift; it grows when s grows, so the more a shape leans the longer its perimeter
the most leaning shape has the longest perimeter and the least leaning the shortest; the book's figure was not in the text, so no letters are named
video_script.design: One row of parallelograms all video. Area is settled by base and height, and the perimeter is settled by the slanting sides.
open_questions: The worklist names (g) as the longest perimeter and (a) as the shortest. The picture is not in the extracted text, so the video says the one that leans most and the one that leans least.

narration: <bookmark mark='area'/>The area of a parallelogram is its base times its height.
<bookmark mark='perim'/>The perimeter is the distance all the way round the shape.
<bookmark mark='sides'/>A parallelogram has two bases and two slanting sides, and each pair is equal.

beats.on_screen: Given: seven parallelograms on equal bases, between the same two grid lines

marks.lines: the two grid lines are highlighted

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, seven parallelograms stand on equal bases.
<bookmark mark='lines'/>All of them lie between the same two grid lines.

beats.on_screen: To find: how the areas compare, how the perimeters compare, and which shape has the longest and the shortest perimeter

marks.find: the things to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to compare their areas and their perimeters.
We also look for the longest and the shortest perimeter.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: same base, same height, so area = base × height is the same for every shape

marks.same: the equal bases are ticked on every shape
marks.ht: the equal heights are ticked on every shape
marks.area: area = base × height is written once for all the shapes

narration: <bookmark mark='same'/>Step one, look at the base and the height of each shape.
<bookmark mark='ht'/>The bases are equal, and the grid lines stay the same distance apart, so every height is equal.
<bookmark mark='area'/>Base times height is the same each time, so the areas are equal.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: perimeter = 2 × base + 2 × slanting side; the bases are equal, so only the slanting sides change it

marks.perim: perimeter = 2 × base + 2 × slanting side is written
marks.cmp: the equal bases are greyed out and the slanting sides glow

narration: <bookmark mark='perim'/>Step two, the perimeter is two bases plus two slanting sides.
<bookmark mark='cmp'/>The bases are equal in every shape, so only the slanting sides can change it.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: slanting side, height and sideways shift make a right triangle; the more the shape leans, the longer the shift and the slanting side

marks.tri: a right triangle is drawn on the slanting side with the height and the shift as its legs
marks.shift: the shift grows as the shape leans over
marks.long: the slanting side grows with it

narration: <bookmark mark='tri'/>Step three, a slanting side is the long side of a right triangle.
Its other two sides are the height, which never changes, and the sideways shift.
<bookmark mark='shift'/>The shift grows as the shape leans, so the slanting side grows too.
<bookmark mark='long'/>The more it leans, the longer its perimeter.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: check by counting squares after moving the cut pieces, and by measuring the slanting sides with a ruler

marks.chk: two shapes are shown with their cut pieces moved to make equal rectangles
marks.ruler: a ruler measures the slanting sides of the upright and the leaning shape

narration: <bookmark mark='chk'/>Step four, check it. Cut and move a piece in two shapes, and count the squares. The counts match.
<bookmark mark='ruler'/>Measure the slanting sides with a ruler. The leaning shape has the longer ones.

beats.on_screen: Answer: all the parallelograms have equal areas; the perimeters differ, longest for the most leaning shape, shortest for the least leaning
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>All the parallelograms have equal areas.
Their perimeters differ. The one that leans most has the longest perimeter, and the one that leans least has the shortest.
